extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers, teacher educators, and curriculum designers
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for judging classroom interventions aimed at teaching proof and proving: assesses their aims, design features, contextual fit, and capacity for sustained, scalable curricular change. Focused on empirical interventions in school/university mathematics instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to change classroom culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how the intervention presents capacity to change the classroom culture (i.e., norms, expectations, and social practices around proof and proving).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The commentary highlights contributions and promise of interventions in terms of changing classroom culture; evaluators should look for evidence that patterns of discussion, norms for justification, and shared practices around proof have shifted. Consider whether interventions alter teacher-student interactions, peer norms, and typical classroom discourse about proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to change the curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how the intervention can influence curricular content, sequencing, or official curricular goals related to proof and proving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess if the intervention's goals and materials can be integrated into existing curricula or lead to curricular revisions. Look for alignment (or misalignment) with standards, scope and sequence, and the potential for adoption beyond pilot contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity to change instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how the intervention affects classroom instruction — the methods, tasks, and teacher practices used when teaching proof and proving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine concrete changes to instructional routines, tasks enacted, teacher questioning and scaffolding, and assessment practices. Consider required teacher knowledge and whether professional development is needed to sustain instructional changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intervention aim: preparedness/competence versus appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the work aims primarily to enhance students’ preparedness for and competence in proof and proving, or explicitly to foster appreciation for the need and importance of proof and proving (or both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish interventions focused on procedural competence and skill development from those targeting epistemic appreciation, motivation, or valuing of proof. Evaluate intended outcomes, measures used, and whether affective/attitudinal goals are addressed alongside competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amenability to scaling up
rubrics_metrics.description: How amenable the intervention is to scaling up from research/pilot settings to broader implementation across classrooms or schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider resource requirements, complexity, dependency on specialized personnel, and fidelity-of-implementation challenges. Look for evidence of replication, adaptability across contexts, and requirements for support (materials, PD, leadership).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practicability for curricular integration
rubrics_metrics.description: How practicable the intervention is for integration into existing curricula and school structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess compatibility with time constraints, standards (e.g., Common Core), assessment regimes, and teachers' existing workloads. Evaluate whether the intervention can be embedded into typical units or requires curriculum-wide restructuring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capability to produce long-lasting effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the intervention is capable of producing durable, sustained effects on student learning, attitudes, or classroom practice over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for follow-up/longitudinal data, maintenance of gains after the intervention ends, and evidence that changes persist across contexts or cohorts. Consider what supports are needed to sustain effects (ongoing PD, curriculum materials, institutionalization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of enhancement of student learning in proof and proving
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the intervention demonstrates potential to enhance student learning related to proof and proving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate empirical outcomes reported (e.g., gains in proof competence, reasoning quality, use of examples), the measures used, effect sizes, and whether multiple strands of evidence (qualitative and quantitative) support claims of learning improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and design variability (student population, content domain, goals, duration, theoretical perspectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attention to how interventions vary by student population, content domain, goals and duration of the intervention, and theoretical perspectives — factors that affect generalizability and fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note variation across these axes; evaluators should consider transferability by interrogating participant characteristics (age, prior knowledge), topical fit (algebra, geometry, analysis), intervention length, and the theoretical framing that shaped design and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design affordances for influencing learning to prove
rubrics_metrics.description: The ways in which classroom experiences are designed to positively influence students’ learning to prove (task design, use of examples, argumentation structures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although discussed at a high level in the commentary, evaluators should look for concrete design features (types of tasks, role of examples, scaffolding of argumentation) and theoretical rationales linking those features to learning goals.
